# Evidence: what is shown, what is practice, what is folklore

Strength scale:

- **Measured**: a stated sample and method, peer reviewed or with its data shown.
- **Survey**: a stated sample, self-reported, often by a party with something to sell. The sign can be used; the
  size cannot.
- **Practice**: a named expert's documented method. Nobody measured it.
- **Untraced**: repeated widely, no source found, or the source does not say it.

Every source is in `sources.md`.

## About personas themselves

| Claim | Source | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| A description with many attributes describes almost nobody: at 9 or more attributes the best 1% of descriptions match no one in 5 of 6 real datasets | Chapman et al. 2008 | Measured (5 of 6 datasets are consumer; one business) |
| Personas cannot be falsified, so their accuracy cannot be shown | Chapman and Milham 2006 | Practice (a reasoned argument, peer reviewed) |
| The paper that set the industrial method measured nothing about its effect | Pruitt and Grudin 2003, own words | Measured (an admission) |
| Practitioners report keeping a persona's role information and ignoring the personal detail | Matthews, Judge and Whittaker 2012 (interviews, 14 design practitioners) | Practitioner reports (qualitative, n=14); not measured on message writing |
| Teams name personas while planning and rarely while deciding | Friess 2012; Ronkko 2005 | Measured (qualitative, small) |
| The value of personas for marketing has not been systematically studied | Kaate et al. 2023 | Measured (statement about the field by its main research group) |
| A persona is not a job title: one title can hold two personas, one persona can span many titles | Goodwin 2001 | Practice |
| Personas are split by goals, tasks and behaviour, not demographics | Cooper 2008 (1995 project); Goodwin 2002; Revella 2016 | Practice, three sources agree |
| With no research, write a "provisional persona": a few goals, one or two traits, no narrative, labelled as a guess | Goodwin 2002 | Practice |
| Detail implies evidence: a precise card claims you observed that precision | Goodwin 2002 | Practice |
| Model-made personas almost always carry demographics; half the studies of them evaluate nothing; the same model writing and judging is circular | Salminen, Amin and Jansen 2025; Amin et al. 2025 | Measured (reviews of the literature) |
| An anti-persona (who you are NOT writing to) is part of the original industrial method | Pruitt and Grudin 2003 | Practice |

## How many personas

| Claim | Source | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| "Three to seven personas" | traced by Salminen et al. 2021 to one 2002 case study | Untraced as a rule |
| Coverage of a user base kept improving up to 40 personas | Salminen et al. 2022 | Measured, but on demographic coverage of video viewers, not on messaging. Does not transfer |
| "Three or fewer distinct personas that really matter" | ITSMA | Practice |
| Merge a persona whose needs are a subset of another's | Goodwin 2002 | Practice |
| Insight-based personas need "half as many" as demographic ones | Revella 2016 | Untraced (her own claim, no data shown) |
| More than about 10 becomes hard to use | Nielsen and Hansen 2014 | Survey (interviews) |
| Microsoft had over 200 personas in use, some teams 50 | Chapman and Milham 2006, personal observation | Untraced (unpublished internal observation) |

Practical conclusion, ours: a new persona earns its place only when it needs a different first message. For one
seller that is 2 to 4. This is a judgement built on the practice rows above, not a measurement.

## What a persona card should hold

| Field | Source | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| What makes them spend time, budget or political capital now (priority initiative), and it is not the same as a pain | Revella 2016 | Practice |
| The result they expect, in their words (success factors) | Revella 2016 | Practice |
| Why they would say no (perceived barriers, "the bad news insight") | Revella 2016 | Practice |
| Their own words, quoted | Revella 2016 | Practice |
| Push of the current situation, pull of the new, anxiety about the new, habit of the present; a switch happens when push plus pull beat anxiety plus habit | Moesta and Spiek, jobstobedone.org | Practice |
| Jobs (functional, social, emotional), pains, gains | Osterwalder et al. 2014 | Practice |
| Two jobs per reader: the company's and their own (credit, promotion, not being blamed) | Romaniuk 2022 | Practice, framed inside a survey report |
| A situation in the form "when ..., I want to ..., so I can ..." | Klement / Intercom job stories | Practice |
| Goal first, then what they see, say, do, hear, think and feel | Gray 2017 | Practice |
| A deadline event (critical event) that makes it urgent | Winning by Design, SPICED | Practice |
| Match the message to what the reader already knows (awareness) | Schwartz 1966 | Practice; the five modern labels are unverified as his wording |
| Demographics, hobbies, age, a photo | Revella ("pictures don't talk"); Matthews 2012; Goodwin | Leave out. Practitioners report ignoring it (Matthews, qualitative, n=14); model-made personas add it by default (Salminen and Jansen reviews); practice everywhere else |

## What moves a cold message

| Claim | Source | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| Executives do not care if you mention their alma mater; reference business problems, not personal fun facts | 30MPC with Gong, 85M+ emails | Survey-like vendor data, method not published |
| Pitch words lower reply rates; prospect-focused language ("you") does better than "we" language | 30MPC with Gong | Vendor data, method not published |
| "Pitching reduces replies by up to 57%" | Jason Bay video summary, likely from the same report | Untraced as a figure |
| Relevance (role and context) beats personalisation (facts about the person) when no real personal premise exists | Becc Holland | Practice |
| Lead with a question that surfaces a problem the reader has not named, not a pitch | Josh Braun | Practice |
| Positioning value to one individual stakeholder: -4% in likelihood of a high-quality sale; collective learning: +20% | CEB 2015 deck | Survey, sample not printed for these charts |
| Individual-level relevance hurts buying-group consensus ("59% negative impact"); group relevance makes a high-quality deal three times more likely | Gartner 2025, n=632 buyers | Survey; relative figures with no base; measured inside active purchases, not at a cold first touch |
| Companies that beat goals are 2x more likely to have personas | Cintell 2016, n=137 self-selected | Survey; correlation, sold as cause downstream. Do not quote |

Practical conclusion, ours: write to the role's problem and its stakes for the team, not to facts about the
person. A persona card at the level of a role and a situation is the right grain. It is also exactly what fixes
"I saw you are X": the title is a way to find the card, never the content of the message.

## Addressing the reader (formal or informal)

| Claim | Source | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| Informal address works better for warm brands, formal for competent ones | Leung et al. 2023, five studies | Measured (consumers, abstract read) |
| German sales talk: du or Sie made no substantial difference overall; where it did, Sie was rated better; du gave no sales advantage | Kretzenbacher and Hensel-Boerner 2024; Hensel-Boerner and Kords 2021 | Measured (perception, summary read) |
| German and French participants rated recruiters higher with the formal pronoun | MDPI address terms special issue 2024 | Measured (summary read) |
| No study tests formal against informal address on B2B reply rates | our search, 2026-10-29 | Absence of evidence |

Practical conclusion, ours, and a default to test rather than a finding: in languages with a formal form, open
formal unless the persona's own world clearly speaks informally (their posts, their sector's norm, a shared
community) or the seller's brand is warm and informal (Leung), and mirror the reader once they reply. The skill
checks address in its per-persona results.

## Buying groups and roles

| Claim | Source | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| Buying group size has no constant: 4.8 to 23 across publishers, the count follows the counting rule | September research, 15 sources compared | Measured (as a comparison) |
| User, buyer, influencer, decider, gatekeeper | Webster and Wind 1972 | Practice (conceptual model, never tested as a partition) |
| Seven stakeholder types (Go-Getter, Teacher, Skeptic, Friend, Guide, Climber, Blocker) | CEB, The Challenger Customer 2015 | Survey-based typology; a personality trait not visible on a profile, so not usable to sort leads |

## Sorting leads into personas

| Claim | Source | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| A model sorts job titles into broad functions with about 92.6% accuracy (500 checked) | arXiv 2506.23230 | Measured (summary read; Chinese listed firms) |
| Default occupation labels in a resume dataset were about 63% accurate | FewSOC, arXiv 2511.12010 | Measured (summary read) |
| Title alone cannot settle a persona; behaviour and situation can split one title | Goodwin 2001 | Practice |

Practical conclusion, ours: sort on title plus company type plus what the person writes about, say why in one
line, and mark "unsure" instead of forcing a fit. The user checks the unsure ones.
